## Margin comparison: AMD vs. NVDA

Note on calendars: AMD reports on a Dec-ending fiscal year; NVDA's fiscal year ends in late January. The quarters below are aligned as closely as the filings allow but are not identical periods.

### Gross margin (from `get_ratios`, quarterly)

| AMD period end | GM | NVDA period end | GM |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2024-09-28 | 50.1% | 2024-10-27 | 74.6% |
| 2024-12-28 *(derived Q4)* | 50.7% | 2025-01-26 *(derived Q4)* | 73.0% |
| 2025-03-29 | 50.2% | 2025-04-27 | 60.5% |
| 2025-06-28 | 39.8% | 2025-07-27 | 72.4% |
| 2025-09-27 | 51.7% | 2025-10-26 | 73.4% |
| 2025-12-27 *(derived Q4)* | 54.3% | 2026-01-25 *(derived Q4)* | 75.0% |
| 2026-03-28 | 52.8% | 2026-04-26 | 74.9% |
| 2026-06-27 | 53.8% | — | — |

The Q4 figures marked *derived* are synthesized (FY minus Q1–Q3), not directly filed quarterly facts — AMD's from the 2026-02-04 filing, NVDA's from 2026-02-25.

### Operating and net margin (most recent quarters)

| | AMD 2026-06-27 | NVDA 2026-04-26 |
|---|---|---|
| Operating margin | 17.25% (op. income $1.990B on $11.536B rev) | 65.60% (op. income $53.536B on $81.615B rev) |
| Net margin | 19.91% ($2.297B) | 71.46% ($58.321B) |
| Revenue growth YoY | 50.1% | 85.2% |

### What the trend shows

**Both took a one-quarter hit and both recovered.** Anomaly detection on gross-profit growth flags AMD's quarter ended 2025-06-28 as a genuine break from its own trend (−18.1% QoQ gross profit, −2.38 trailing std devs) — gross margin fell to 39.8% and operating margin went *negative* (−1.74%, operating loss of $134M). The following quarter, 2025-09-27, is flagged in the opposite direction (+56.3% QoQ, +3.90 std devs) as it snapped back to 51.7%.

NVDA's comparable dip is the quarter ended 2025-04-27: gross margin 60.5% vs. 73.0% the prior quarter, operating margin 49.1%, net margin 42.6%. Notably, that quarter was *not* flagged as a statistical anomaly (−1.24 std devs) — NVDA's baseline volatility is wide enough to absorb it, and it recovered to 72.4% the very next quarter.

**Direction of travel:**
- AMD is on a genuine, multi-quarter improvement: gross margin from 46.8% (2024-03-30) to 53.8% (2026-06-27), and operating margin from 0.66% to 17.25% over the same span. That's real operating leverage — margins expanding meaningfully faster than the gross line.
- NVDA is not expanding gross margin so much as holding an extraordinarily high one: 74.6% → 74.9% across roughly two years, with the export-charge quarter as the only interruption. Its operating margin, however, has climbed to 65.60% from 62.3% (2024-10-27), and net margin to 71.46% — the latter above operating margin, which points to non-operating income rather than core-operations improvement.

### Who's "better positioned"

The data supports two different readings, and they don't resolve to a single answer:

- **On absolute margin structure, NVDA is not close to being matched.** Its worst gross-margin quarter in the window (60.5%) is still above AMD's best (54.3%). Its operating margin is roughly four times AMD's.
- **On margin *trajectory*, AMD has the steeper improvement curve** — it's the one adding margin points, off a much lower base, while NVDA's gross margin is essentially flat at a high plateau. AMD is also the more volatile: it printed a negative operating margin as recently as the quarter ended 2025-06-28.
- **On growth, NVDA still leads** — 85.2% YoY revenue growth (2026-04-26) vs. AMD's 50.1% (2026-06-27), despite NVDA's far larger base.

Market pricing (Yahoo Finance, as of 2026-08-21, not SEC data) reflects the trajectory-vs-level split: AMD trades at a trailing P/E of 118.3 and EV/EBITDA of 78.7; NVDA at a trailing P/E of 33.1 and EV/EBITDA of 31.6. Forward P/Es are 30.0 and 16.7 respectively. AMD carries the far richer multiple on current earnings — the improvement is priced in.

I'm reporting what the filings show rather than making a recommendation. One caveat worth flagging: the recovery quarters for both companies follow inventory/export-related charges, so the pre- and post-dip margin levels are the cleaner comparison than the dip quarters themselves.
